extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena) under the Alice/Mayo two-part framework, including machine-or-transformation, extra-solution activity, well-understood/routine/conventional activity, and meaningful limitation considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the machine or apparatus implements the steps of the method
rubrics_metrics.description: Integral use of a machine to achieve performance of a method may provide significantly more, in contrast to where the machine is merely an object on which the method operates, which does not provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machine must play a significant part in permitting the claimed method to be performed rather than function solely as an obvious mechanism for permitting a solution to be achieved more quickly. Mere recitation that a method 'would not be necessary or possible without the Internet' is insufficient (CyberSource; Versata examples). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for related discussion on mere instructions to apply an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether its involvement is extra-solution activity or a field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the extent to which the machine or apparatus imposes meaningful limits on the claim versus contributing only nominally or insignificantly (e.g., data gathering or field-of-use limitation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the machine's contribution is nominal or merely identifies a source of data (e.g., the Internet), it will not provide 'significantly more'. See Bilski, CyberSource and MPEP § 2106.05(g) & (h) for more on insignificant extra-solution activity and field of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Transformation (M-or-T) consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing — a clue to patentability of a process claim that does not include particular machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation of an article is an important clue but not a stand-alone test. All claims must be evaluated under Alice/Mayo; satisfying M-or-T alone is not sufficient (Bilski; Diamond v. Diehr examples). See the five factors below for evaluating a recited transformation and consider other Step 2B factors (MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 1: Particularity or generality of the transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: How definite or particular the transformation is — more particular transformations are more likely to provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court examples (tanning, dyeing, smelting) show that transformations that confine the patent monopoly within definite bounds are favorable (Gottschalk v. Benson, Corning v. Burden). A more particular transformation likely supports eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 2: Degree to which the recited article is particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the transformation applies to a specifically identified article or to generically recited or any and all articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformations applied to generically recited articles or to 'any and all' articles are less likely to provide significantly more; specificity (particular articles) favors eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 3: Nature of the transformation (type/extent of change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the type or extent of change in state or thing resulting from the claimed transformation (e.g., new function/use versus mere change of location).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformations that yield a new function or use are more likely to provide significantly more; mere relocation is unlikely to. Example: process transforming raw synthetic rubber into precision-molded products (Diamond v. Diehr) provides significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 4: Nature of the article transformed
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the transformed article is physical/tangible versus intangible (e.g., contractual obligation or mental judgment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation of a physical or tangible object/substance is more likely to provide significantly more than transformation of an intangible concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 5: Whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or a field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claimed transformation merely imposes field-of-use limits or otherwise contributes only nominally to execution of the claimed method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the transformation is only a field-of-use limitation or nominal activity (e.g., administering a drug where administration was treated as only a field-of-use in Mayo), it likely does not provide significantly more. See MPEP § 2106.05(g) & (h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the additional element(s) are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry. If so, recitation at a high level generally does not favor eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional element(s) are specific and unconventional (confine claim to particular useful application), they can favor eligibility (e.g., DDR Holdings). If elements are well-understood/routine/conventional and recited at a high level, they typically do not amount to 'significantly more' (e.g., Mayo). Examiner should rely on what courts or those of ordinary skill recognize, and need not perform a prior art search; expertise/judicial notice may suffice. Combinations of conventional elements can nonetheless amount to an inventive concept (Diehr, Rapid Litigation, BASCOM). The specification may indicate conventionality (e.g., described as 'well-known' or 'conventional'). See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner reliance on expertise vs prior art search for conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner should conclude additional elements are well-understood/routine/conventional only when they can readily conclude that the element is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant industry without needing a prior art search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an element is not widely prevalent or common use, or beyond those recognized by courts/the art, it will in most cases favor eligibility. Example: a niche technique used by a few scientists does not make it routine/conventional in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination may be inventive despite conventional parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual additional elements are well-understood/routine/conventional, their combination may amount to an inventive concept that provides significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New combinations of known steps or non-conventional arrangements of generic components (e.g., BASCOM, Rapid Litigation) may yield eligibility; examiners should consider elements individually and in combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer function: Receiving or transmitting data over a network
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving or transmitting data over a network (e.g., using the Internet to gather data) has been recognized as a well-understood, routine, conventional activity when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Symantec, TLI Communications, OIP Technologies, buySAFE. Exception: DDR Holdings where specific manipulation of Internet interactions yielded a technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer function: Performing repetitive calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing repetitive calculations on a computer is a basic, conventional use of a computer and, when claimed generically, is often considered routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Flook; Bancorp Services—computers employed only for repetitive calculations do not impose meaningful limits on claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer function: Electronic recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating, updating, or maintaining electronic records (e.g., 'shadow accounts', activity logs) is a well-recognized conventional computer function when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Alice Corp., Ultramercial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer function: Storing and retrieving information in memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic storing and retrieving data in memory is recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional activity when recited at a high level of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Versata Dev. Group v. SAP, OIP Techs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer function: Electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document
rubrics_metrics.description: Optical character recognition or extracting data from documents is treated as a conventional activity when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: Content Extraction and Transmission v. Wells Fargo (OCR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer function: Web browser navigation functions (back/forward)
rubrics_metrics.description: Browser back and forward button functionality is an example of a generic computer function that courts have treated as well-understood/routine when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: Internet Patent Corp. v. Active Network.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-science technique: Determining level of a biomarker in blood by any means
rubrics_metrics.description: Measuring biomarker levels in blood is a recognized well-understood, routine, conventional activity when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Mayo; Cleveland Clinic Foundation v. True Health Diagnostics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-science technique: Using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify and detect DNA
rubrics_metrics.description: Using PCR to amplify/detect DNA is a well-understood, routine, conventional laboratory technique when claimed at a high level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Genetic Technologies v. Merial; Ariosa Diagnostics v. Sequenom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-science technique: Detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample
rubrics_metrics.description: Detection of DNA or enzymes in a sample is treated as conventional activity when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Sequenom; Cleveland Clinic Foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-science technique: Immunizing a patient against a disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Immunization of a patient is a recognized conventional technique in certain contexts when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: Classen Immunotherapies v. Biogen IDEC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-science technique: Analyzing DNA to provide sequence information or detect allelic variants
rubrics_metrics.description: DNA sequencing/analysis to obtain sequence information or detect variants is a conventional laboratory activity when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: Genetic Technologies; Ambry Genetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-science technique: Freezing and thawing cells
rubrics_metrics.description: Freezing and thawing cells is a conventional laboratory activity; however, non-routine repetition contrary to the art may be inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: Rapid Litigation Management v. CellzDirect (repeating steps contrary to art was non-routine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-science technique: Amplifying and sequencing nucleic acid sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplifying and sequencing nucleic acids is recognized as conventional when recited generically in claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: University of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-science technique: Hybridizing a gene probe
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybridization of gene probes is a conventional laboratory technique when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: Ambry Genetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conventional activity: Recording a customer's order
rubrics_metrics.description: Recording a customer's order has been recognized as a conventional activity when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: Apple v. Ameranth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conventional activity: Shuffling and dealing a standard deck of cards
rubrics_metrics.description: Shuffling and dealing a standard deck of cards is an example of an activity courts have recognized as conventional when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: In re Smith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conventional activity: Restricting public access to media by requiring a consumer to view an advertisement
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring a consumer to view an advertisement as a prerequisite to access content can be a conventional activity when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: Ultramercial v. Hulu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conventional activity: Identifying undeliverable mail items and decoding/creating output
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying undeliverable mail, decoding data on mail items, and creating output data has been recognized as conventional when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: Return Mail, Inc. v. U.S. Postal Service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conventional activity: Presenting offers and gathering statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting offers and gathering statistics is an example of conventional activity when claimed at a high level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: OIP Technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conventional activity: Determining an estimated outcome and setting a price
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining an estimated outcome and using it to set a price is recognized as conventional activity when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: OIP Technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conventional activity: Arranging hierarchy, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing information and determining price
rubrics_metrics.description: Arranging hierarchical groups, sorting information and determining pricing based on that sorting can be conventional when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: Versata Dev. Group v. SAP America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Meaningful Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim directed to a judicial exception must include additional features that ensure the claim applies the exception in a meaningful way—i.e., add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the exception to a technological environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaningful limitations are those that amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (e.g., Diehr's mold-closing, temperature-measuring, automatic opening steps). Mere recitation of implementation on computers or well-understood routine activity recited at a high level does not meaningfully limit (Alice). Consider additional elements individually and in combination; specification and case law (Diehr, Classen, OIP, DDR Holdings) provide examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere Instructions To Apply An Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the additional elements are nothing more than mere instructions to apply the judicial exception (i.e., 'apply it' or 'implement on a generic computer').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim simply states the judicial exception while adding words to 'apply it', that does not transform the exception into patent-eligible subject matter (Alice; Mayo; Benson examples). Examiners should treat recitations of generic computers that merely implement an abstract idea as mere instructions to apply the exception.
